version_history.subject: [PATCH v4] mm: bypass swap readahead for zswap

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch bypasses swap readahead for zswap, an in-memory, synchronous backend similar to zram. The current implementation of swap readahead is optimized for disk-based swaps and can cause unnecessary page cache thrashing and compression traffic when used with in-memory swaps like zswap. By bypassing readahead for zswap, the patch aims to reduce memory usage, improve performance, and decrease compression overhead. The results show significant gains in build time, reduced swap-in and -out rates, and a substantial reduction in swap readahead pages. The patch is based on measurements from various systems and configurations.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/1] mm/swap: allocate contiguous swap slots for a reclaim batch
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes swap slot allocation by allocating contiguous slots in batches, reducing the number of small write requests and improving performance. It achieves this by recording the number of pages of each order that need a slot before swapping out a batch, and then making those allocations follow contiguous free slots. This approach helps to minimize the fragmentation of swap clusters and reduces the overhead of small write requests.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concerns that the patch does not address workloads that benefit more from disk swapping than compression swapping, and requested further consideration for these use cases.

Reviewer noted that the patch does not apply its contiguous allocation heuristic to folios larger than a certain order, and found this omission reasonable.

Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concern that the patch's preference for non-full clusters with contiguous slots may lead to increased lock contention, especially as swapfiles become more fragmented.

Reviewer Nhat Pham raised concerns about the effectiveness of the contiguous swap slot allocation heuristic, questioning whether it would lead to overshooting the estimate and creating problems down the line. They also suggested that this heuristic might not be necessary for cgroups that enable zswap or zram.
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks for looking into this! There are still workloads that benefit
more from disk swapping than compression swapping... We should make
the swap subsystem work for them.

I haven't read the code too closely, as it's an RFC meant to show the
general idea. So I'll just make some comments and ask some questions
about the idea:

---

Ah so we don't invoke this heuristics for folio larger than certain
orders? Makes sense.

---

So we prefer non-full clusters with contiguous slots, over free
clusters, over other nonfull clusters.

I think this part makes sense to me FWIW. We do skip fast path and go
for slow paths more often, so do make sure we're not paying with too
much lock contention, especially as the swapfile fils or get more
fragmented (which this patch series does nudge us towards). But FWIW,
we pretty much go back to the old behavior the moment we fail to find
contiguity for the first time in the batch, so I think we'll be
fine...?

---

Some general questions:

1. How many pages in folio_list typically do get reclaimed? There can
be quite a few with references, which we rotate/promote, when we scan,
right? Would constantly overshooting the estimate create problem down
the line?

(This is one of the few places where indirection (vswap) would have
helped - we can collect a batch of pages after unmapping, then pass
them to the phys swap allocator (after checking zswappability, etc.).
Maybe we can solve it better after it's landed, and accept an
imperfect solution for now?)

2. Should we skip this heuristics for cgroups that enables zswap (and
maybe zram)? Contiguity matters less there... unless it help at
writeback time? Hard to say without experimentation - maybe you can do
the same check you did for your zswap writeback batching patch series?

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch aims to reduce the number of I/O requests on a swap device by keeping reclaim batches contiguous. The current implementation of swap allocation and deallocation can lead to scattered writes, resulting in increased I/O requests. The patch modifies the allocator to allocate contiguous free slots for a reclaim batch, reducing the number of small requests and improving throughput. This is achieved by informing the allocator about the size of the batch and allowing it to allocate contiguous slots accordingly. The goal is to reduce the overhead of swap I/O operations and improve system performance.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 01/12] mm/page_alloc: reset can_retry_reserves when the slowpath restarts
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the page allocation slowpath by resetting can_retry_reserves when it restarts after a cpuset update or zonelist rebuild. This change ensures that the retry still runs at most once per change, preventing unnecessary retries and improving allocation success rates.

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Identified the need for resetting can_retry_reserves on restart to prevent unnecessary retries and improve allocation success rates. Approved the patch with Acked-by.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Sat Oct 31, 2026 at 10:13 PM EDT, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> Commit 2c4c3e29897d ("mm/page_alloc: simplify __alloc_pages_slowpath()
> flow") retries an allocation once with reserve_flags when the caller
> becomes eligible for reserves, guarded by can_retry_reserves.
>
> A restart after a cpuset update or a zonelist rebuild retries with
> can_retry_reserves already set to false, so a caller that cannot
> reclaim (GFP_NOWAIT | __GFP_MEMALLOC), fails without trying reserves.
>
> Reset can_retry_reserves on restart. Only a cpuset or zonelist change
> restarts the slowpath, so the retry still runs at most once per change.
>
> With a kprobe helping to make the race deterministic, an allocation
> can be made to return NULL. With this patch the allocation will succeed.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 02/12] mm/page_alloc: keep the pagesets of an empty zone
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a memory leak in the Linux kernel by keeping the pagesets of an empty zone instead of freeing them when the last memory of a zone goes offline. The current implementation frees the per-cpu pageset and zonestats, which can lead to corruption if the per-cpu memory has been reassigned. This patch series modifies the setup_zone_pageset() function to reuse existing pagesets when a zone is repopulated.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 03/12] mm, page_alloc: pass zone pointer to trace_reclaim_retry_zone
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series modifies the page allocation code to pass a zone pointer instead of a zoneref pointer to the trace_reclaim_retry_zone tracepoint, addressing an issue where memory hotplug rebuilds the zonelists in place while allocations are under way. The change ensures that the correct zone is referenced even when entries move up due to empty zones.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 04/12] mm/page_alloc: detect zonelist rebuilds from memory hot-add
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a race condition between build_all_zonelists and page allocation by detecting zonelist rebuilds from memory hot-add. The fix involves gating sequence checks on CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG, which covers every configuration that rebuilds zonelists after boot.

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Acknowledged the patch with Acked-by, indicating agreement to apply it.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Sat Oct 31, 2026 at 10:13 PM EDT, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> The zonelist_update_seq retry was limited to CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE,
> presumably because only hot-remove takes zones out of a zonelist.
>
> However, build_zonerefs_node() rewrites the zonelists in place, so
> onlining the first block of a zone shifts the entries that follow it
> in every zonelist containing that zone.  This can cause a spurious
> allocation failure for a __GFP_THISNODE caller.
>
> For a node with only ZONE_NORMAL, onlining its first ZONE_MOVABLE block
> rewrites the node's ZONELIST_NOFALLBACK list as:
>
>   [NORMAL, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NORMAL, NULL]
>
> A concurrent GFP_KERNEL | __GFP_THISNODE allocation can observe the
> intermediate list, skip ZONE_MOVABLE, and find no eligible zone. With
> CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE=n, check_retry_zonelist() returns 0 and the
> allocation fails even though the node has free ZONE_NORMAL memory.
>
> Gate the sequence checks on CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG, which covers every
> configuration that rebuilds zonelists after boot.
>
> Fixes: 3d36424b3b58 ("mm/page_alloc: fix race condition between build_all_zonelists and page allocation")

series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a memory hotplug issue where zonelists are rebuilt in place, causing potential double-put bugs when accessing the zoneref slot. It uses READ_ONCE() to ensure that the zone is loaded only once.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 06/12] mm/page_alloc: snapshot the preferred zone against shrink rebuilds
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a kernel NULL pointer dereference bug in the page allocation code. The issue arises from concurrent zonelist rebuilds that can null or replace the preferred zone slot, leading to a crash when trying to access it. From: Josef Bacik <josef@toxicpanda.com>

should_reclaim_retry() walks a zonelist and passes the zoneref pointer
to the reclaim_retry_zone tracepoint, which loads the zone from the
entry again to find the node.

Memory hotplug rebuilds the zonelists in place while allocations are
under way. When a zone in front of the zoneref entry has become empty,
the entries move up, and this one can be the end marker by the time the
tracepoint looks at it. zonelist_node_idx() then dereferences a NULL
zone. Short of that, the event can name another zone than the one its
numbers belong to.

review_comments.author: Gregory (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern that the zonelist_update_seq retry was limited to CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE, but this led to spurious allocation failures for __GFP_THISNODE callers when onlining zones. The author agreed to gate the sequence checks on CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG instead.
review_comments.raw_body:
The zonelist_update_seq retry was limited to CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE,
presumably because only hot-remove takes zones out of a zonelist.

However, build_zonerefs_node() rewrites the zonelists in place, so
onlining the first block of a zone shifts the entries that follow it
in every zonelist containing that zone.  This can cause a spurious
allocation failure for a __GFP_THISNODE caller.

For a node with only ZONE_NORMAL, onlining its first ZONE_MOVABLE block
rewrites the node's ZONELIST_NOFALLBACK list as:

  [NORMAL, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NORMAL, NULL]

A concurrent GFP_KERNEL | __GFP_THISNODE allocation can observe the
intermediate list, skip ZONE_MOVABLE, and find no eligible zone. With
CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE=n, check_retry_zonelist() returns 0 and the
allocation fails even though the node has free ZONE_NORMAL memory.

Gate the sequence checks on CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG, which covers every
configuration that rebuilds zonelists after boot.

Fixes: 3d36424b3b58 ("mm/page_alloc: fix race condition between build_all_zonelists and page allocation")

index e14d550d4128..11be12b443ad 100644
--- a/mm/page_alloc.c
+++ b/mm/page_alloc.c
@@ -4404,7 +4404,7 @@ static DEFINE_SEQLOCK(zonelist_update_seq);

 {
-	if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE))
+	if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG))
 		return read_seqbegin(&zonelist_update_seq);
 
 	return 0;
@@ -4412,7 +4412,7 @@ static unsigned int zonelist_iter_begin(void)
 
 static unsigned int check_retry_zonelist(unsigned int seq)
 {
-	if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE))
+	if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG))
 		return read_seqretry(&zonelist_update_seq, seq);

review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern about the swapoff path dropping the per-vswap spinlock before calling try_to_unmap(). They acknowledged that this is necessary to prevent corruption of per-cpu memory, and explained that the pagesets are only freed because setup_zone_pageset() would otherwise leak them. From: Josef Bacik <josef@toxicpanda.com>

When the last memory of a zone goes offline, zone_pcp_reset() frees
zone->per_cpu_pageset and zone->per_cpu_zonestats. Nothing waits for those
who found the zone populated and still use the two pointers. They take
neither the memory hotplug lock nor any other lock which offline_pages()
holds, and some of them can sleep:

  CPU0 vmstat_update()                CPU1 offline_pages()
  refresh_cpu_vm_stats()
    for_each_populated_zone(zone)
      pcp = zone->per_cpu_pageset
      cond_resched()
                                      adjust_present_page_count()
                                      zone_pcp_reset(zone)
                                        free_percpu(zone->per_cpu_pageset)
      decay_pcp_high(zone, pcp)
      __this_cpu_write(pcp->expire, 0)

The same goes for drain_all_pages(NULL), which takes pcp->lock, for
zone_pcp_update(), show_free_areas() and the readers and writers of the
zonestats. If the per-cpu memory has got a new owner in the meantime, it
is corrupted.

The pagesets are only freed because setup_zone_pageset() would otherwise
leak them when the zone gets memory again. Keep them instead and let
setup_zone_pageset() and zone_pcp_init() use them again, like it is done
with pgdat->per_cpu_nodestats. Their lists are empty, and their limits
have been calculated for a zone without memory by the
init_per_zone_wmark_min() of offline_pages(), which is what
setup_zone_pageset() would come up with as well.

review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the compiler reordering loads of a zoneref slot, which could lead to using an incorrect zone or NULL pointer. They proposed using READ_ONCE() to ensure a single load and prevent this issue.
review_comments.raw_body:
Memory hotplug rebuilds zonelists in place while allocations walk them,
so a zoneref slot can change between two loads of it.

zonelist_zone() loads the slot with a plain access.  The compiler may
load it again later instead of keeping the zone it already read, so a
caller can check one zone and then use another, or the NULL terminator.

Use READ_ONCE().  Callers that take a zone from a slot and keep using
it, such as get_page_from_freelist() with ac->preferred_zoneref, need
that single load.

review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the __next_zones_zonelist() function reading a slot twice, which can lead to a NULL pointer dereference when offlining a zone's last block. The author explained that current GCC and clang merge the two reads, but nothing requires it, and provided an example where holding a nodemask allocation between the reads causes an oops. review_comments.raw_body:
__next_zones_zonelist() tests a slot's zone for NULL, then reads the
slot again to look up the zone's node. Offlining a zone's last block
rebuilds the zonelists in place, so the second read can return the
terminator:

  CPU 0                             CPU 1
  __next_zones_zonelist(nodemask)
    zonelist_zone(slot 1) = NORMAL
                                    offline_pages()
                                      build_all_zonelists()
                                        [MOVABLE, NORMAL, NULL]
                                        -> [NORMAL, NULL]
    zref_in_nodemask(slot 1)
      zone_to_nid(NULL)

Current GCC and clang merge the two reads, but nothing requires it.
With mm/mmzone.o built with -fno-inline -fno-ipa-sra, holding a
nodemask allocation between the reads while the node's last movable
block goes offline oopses every time:

  BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000060
  RIP: 0010:zone_to_nid+0x0/0x10
  Call Trace:
   zref_in_nodemask+0x9/0x20
   __next_zones_zonelist+0x23/0x70
   prepare_alloc_pages.constprop.0+0x16c/0x190
   __alloc_frozen_pages_noprof+0xaf/0x330

Read the slot once and test that zone. A NULL zone still ends the walk.

Fixes: 11cd8638c37f ("mm, page_alloc: remove stop_machine from build_all_zonelists")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net>
Reviewed-by: Vlastimil Babka (SUSE) <vbabka@kernel.org>

index 9cc9ef588580..65880396f104 100644
--- a/mm/mmzone.c

@@ -43,13 +43,14 @@ struct zone *next_zone(struct zone *zone)
 	return zone;
 }
 
-static inline int zref_in_nodemask(struct zoneref *zref,
-				   const nodemask_t *nodes)
+/* A NULL zone terminates the zonelist, so it ends the search. */
+static inline bool zone_in_nodemask(const struct zone *zone,
+				    const nodemask_t *nodes)
 {
 #ifdef CONFIG_NUMA
-	return node_isset(zonelist_node_idx(zref), *nodes);
+	return !zone || node_isset(zone_to_nid(zone), *nodes);

-	return 1;

 			z++;

-				(zonelist_zone(z) && !zref_in_nodemask(z, nodes)))

The patch introduces a delayed_work to unblock expired sdevs after a missing delay plus 30 seconds, ensuring that devices are not stuck waiting for the lock. This fix builds upon an earlier partial solution and ensures that LUN 0 is also handled correctly during scans.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series fixes a deadlock issue in the mpt3sas SCSI driver by introducing a timed unblock mechanism for not-responding devices. The deadlock occurs when an interrupt-time block is held while the hostdata teardown is being done, causing a lockup. To fix this, the patch introduces a new lock and ensures that the timed unblock happens under this lock to prevent racing with an interrupt-time block. Additionally, it clears the block deadline before polling a returning device with TURs to prevent mid-poll unblocking.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v1 2/3] mm: memcg: read root lruvec LRU stats from the node counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the accuracy of LRU (Least Recently Used) statistics in the Linux kernel's memory cgroup (memcg) subsystem by reading the root lruvec LRU stats from the node counters instead of relying on potentially stale rstat flushes. This change is particularly important for global reclaim and refault detection, where accurate statistics are crucial. The patch introduces two new functions, `lruvec_lru_page_state` and its monotonic variant, which read the node counters for the root memcg. This approach eliminates the latency introduced by rstat flushes, reducing the time taken to perform root reclaim from approximately 0.9ms to near-zero. The change also improves the accuracy of LRU statistics, ensuring that they reflect the current state of memory allocation and deallocation in the system.

For the root memcg, it's possible to directly read global counters instead of going through rstat, as they are always up-to-date. series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 1/5] mm/memcontrol: flatten try_charge_memcg control flow
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the try_charge_memcg function in mm/memcontrol.c to simplify its control flow by separating the logic for memsw and memory page counters into distinct paths. This makes it easier to follow the code, especially after making page_counter_try_charge stock-aware. The change does not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 2/5] mm/page_counter: introduce per-CPU stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a per-CPU stock representation in the page_counter layer, similar to memcg's seven-slot per-CPU stock. It adds a new struct page_counter_stock_pcp that preserves the existing behavior from memcg and includes a backpointer to the base of the percpu stock. The patch also updates the page_counter structure to include pointers to the percpu stock and its owning cgroup_subsys_state. No functional changes are intended in this patch, which is part of a larger series.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 3/5] mm/page_counter: make page_counter_try_charge() stock-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page_counter_try_charge() function to be aware of stock, allowing it to consume stock transparently while preserving existing semantics. Two new parameters are added: may_batch and nr_charged. The first parameter preserves the behavior of !allow_spinning scenarios in try_charge_memcg, where charges are made as quickly as possible without evicting other stock slots or making a greedy charge to refill the stock. The second parameter reflects the size of the successful hierarchy charge, preserving batch-based memory.high accounting for current->memcg_nr_pages_over_high.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 4/5] mm/memcontrol: move memory stock to page counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the memory stock from memcg to page counters, allowing for more efficient management of memory usage. The change affects how memory and swap counters interact, potentially causing temporary divergence in their raw values. To maintain compatibility, the patch introduces a new logic to ensure that reclaim doesn't swap when memory fails first, even if memory and swap have equal limits. The patch also removes unused memcg code and preserves existing behaviors for cgroup v2 users. The change sets the stage for future work on introducing additional page counters without breaking the fast path.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 5/5] mm/memcontrol: add stock to the memsw page counter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a separate stock to the memsw page counter, allowing it to operate independently of the memory bank. The common drain scheduling is factored into schedule_stock_drain(), which handles charge, refill, and hotplug operations for both stocks. If memory charge fails, only nr_pages from memsw are rolled back. The patch also preserves the user-visible cgroup-v1 memory invariant by reporting memory.usage_in_bytes as the smaller raw value.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series moves the stock management from mem_cgroup to page_counter, allowing each page_counter to have its own per-CPU cache of pre-charged pages. This change is necessary for future work on scalable and performant page_counters, such as the tiered memcg limits series. The decoupling of memory and memsw stocks in cgroup v1 users may lead to different sizes of precharged caches, but the patch preserves the invariant that memory.usage_in_bytes is less than or equal to memory.memsw.usage_in_bytes by reporting the smaller value. This change has no functional impact on memcg v2 users.

> > difficult to add new page_counters to a memcg and preserve the fast
> > path behavior.
> > 
> > This matters for future work like my tiered memcg limits series [1]
> > which introduces multiple new page_counters to memcg. Without making
> > stock a page_counter-level property, it means that every memcg charge
> > now goes through multiple page_counter hierarchy walks, instead of
> > being able to cache these charges.
> > 
> > To make future page_counters scalable and performant, move stock from
> > mem_cgroup to page_counter so that each page_counter can opt into its
> > own per-CPU cache of pre-charged pages.
> 
> What does it mean that each counter can opt into its own per-cpu
> caching?

So right now for cgroupv2, there's kind of a 1-1 mapping between
page_counter and memcg. I say "kind of" because there still is a
page_counter for swap, but it takes a completely different charging
path (i.e. not try_charge_memcg).

This means that currently stocking charge for memcg is equivalent to
stocking charge for the memcg->memory page_counter.

However, one of the series that I'm currently working on [1] adds new
page_counters to struct memcg to track the usage of memory
per-memcg, per-tier. The goal is to (1) track how much memory of a
cgroup lives on which tier, and (2) to limit the usage so that a single
cgroup doesn't use up all the fast tier memory alone, and shares it
fairly with all the other cgroups on the host.

When adding a new per-tier page_counter to struct mem_cgroup that gets
charged for every memcg_charge, I cannot use the stock fastpath since
the stock does not distinguish where the memory resides. It would
essentialy boil down to this pattern:

try_charge_memcg
   \__ page_couner_try_charge(memcg->tier[0])
   \__ consume_stock()

Where every path still has to do a hierarchy charge to the tier it's
charging to, whereas this patch gets us:

try_charge_memcg
   \__ page_counter_try_charge(memcg->tier[0])
          \__ consume_stock(memcg->tier[0])
   \__ page_countertry_charge(memcg->memory)
          \__ consume_stock(memcg->memory)

So that we can avoid the hierarchy walk for most charges.

I'd be happy to submit a new cover letter which better explains this
idea!

> > We get an added benefit of simplifying try_charge_memcg(), which now
> > has all the stock management handled transparently within the
> > page_counter layer.
> 
> This is quite a large change and I believe it will be really benefitial
> to have some high level design overview in the cover rather than trying to
> chase it in respective patches.

Sounds good with me. I can add the call traces above which should
explain my thought process a bit more. Hopefully the problem I am
trying to solve is evident there.

> Namely, are there any changes to the locking (which is arguably quite
> tricky to allow completely lockless fast path)?

No changes to locking. In fact this series is mostly just moving code
from mm/memcontrol.c to mm/page_counter.c, everything is essentially
the same. 

> Also what are implications to caching at different levels of the
> hierarchy? An example of cache propagation up/down the hierarchy during
> charge/uncharge/draining would be really useful to wrap ones head around
> how this is supposed to work.

This series should not have any changes for cgroup v2, including when
and where the cache is stocked / drained in the hierarchy. I can
include a snippet on how stocking currently works to add a visual
explanation, if that helps too.

> > EFFECT ON MEMCG V2 USERS
> > ========================
> > This series has no functional changes intended for memcg v2 users. We
> > preserve all draining, refilling, and (un)charging behavior, including
> > the uncharge path's refills / direct uncharges.

> > to a different size of precharged cache for each.

> > Cgroup v1 has an invariant that memory.memsw.usage_in_bytes is larger
> > than or equal to memory.usage_in_bytes, because memsw is a superset of
> > memory. With separate stocking, this could have been broken in scenarios
> > where the memory stock is bigger than the memsw stock, leading to
> > memory usage appearing to be inflated and greater than memsw usage,
> > even though the real usage preserves the invariant.
> 
> How can this happen when counters are always charged together?

Yeah, so this part is a little bit annoying. Let's just look at a single
leaf cgroup for example, where the limit for memsw and memory are both
64 pages.

charge_memcg(64)
	raw memory: 64			raw memsw: 64
	reported memory: 64		reported memsw: 64
	memory stock: 0			memory stock: 0

swap out 32 pages
	raw memory: 32			raw memsw: 64
	reported memory: 32		reported memsw: 64
	memory stock: 0			memsw stock: 0

free 32 pages
	raw memory: 0			raw memsw: 32
	reported memory: 0		reported memsw: 32
	memory stock: 0			memsw stock: 0

charge_memcg(1)
	raw memory: 1			raw memsw: 33
	reported memory: 64		reported memsw: 33
	memory stock: 63		memsw stock: 0

Where the last charge_memcg() causes the inversion. memsw tries to
charge a batch of 64 to refill the stock, but fails since 32+64=96
puts the memsw over its max limit. So it falls back to direct charging
where it charges the page_counter directly, and ends up with 0 stock
and reporting a usage of 33.

On the other hand, memory will greedily refill the stock with 64 pages
and since usage is 0, the batch refill will succeed, and it will report
a usage of 64.

So the idea with reporting the minimum is to report the minimum of the
two reported values, we will just fuzzily report the stocked value.
IIRC usage_in_bytes has always been fuzzy anyways, due to how much
memory has been stocked.

Thanks again for taking a look, Michal! I hope you have a great day : -)
Joshua

> Michal Hocko
> SUSE Labs

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/3] mm: page_alloc: add a watermark check that knows the migratetype
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a watermark check to the Linux kernel's page allocation system that takes into account the migratetype of the request. The high-order check in __zone_watermark_ok() previously accepted free pages of any migratetype, which could lead to incorrect results under ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT. To fix this, the patch introduces a new function __zone_watermark_ok_mt() that considers only the pages it can take based on the request's migratetype. This change affects various parts of the kernel, including the allocator fast path, recheck after node reclaim, and compaction's up-front check.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm: page_alloc: make the high-order watermark check honour ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the high-order watermark check in the Linux kernel's page allocation system to honor the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT flag when it is set. This flag prevents allocations from stealing pages from other migration types, which can lead to fragmentation and slow down memory allocation under memory pressure. The patch makes two changes: it updates the __zone_watermark_ok_mt function to skip checking free lists of other migration types for ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT requests, and it adds a similar check to the __compact_finished function. This change improves the performance of direct compaction by reducing the number of stalls caused by failed allocations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/3] mm: vmscan: tell direct reclaim the allocation is ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the direct reclaim process in Linux to pass an ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT flag from the allocation down to try_to_free_pages(). This change allows the allocation to take free pages of any migratetype, rather than being restricted to unmovable and reclaimable pageblocks. The goal is to improve performance by reducing fragmentation during high-order direct reclaims. The patch is based on a previous fix for defrag_mode and has been tested with Dev Jain's 64K mTHP benchmark.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a performance issue in Linux kernel's memory management under certain conditions. When defrag_mode is enabled, high-order watermark checks incorrectly count free pages of all migratetypes, leading to inefficient compaction and direct reclaim. The patches modify the watermark check to consider only the request's migratetype and skip free lists that cannot be used for allocation. This change improves performance by reducing compaction stalls and 64K faults under memory pressure.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the follow_page_mask() function in the mm/gup module to return a long integer instead of a struct page pointer. The new return type allows for a page count to be carried by the return value, rather than just a single struct page pointer. The change is made without introducing any functional changes and has been tested with various benchmarks showing no measurable difference.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/8] mm/gup: split out folio grab-and-store helper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch splits out a helper function, gup_grab_folio_pages(), from the follow_page_pte() function in mm/gup.c. The new helper function grabs a folio reference for multiple pages, marks them accessed and dirty if necessary, and stores them for the caller. A separate function, gup_flush_pages(), is introduced to handle cache flushes, which are left to the caller after dropping the page table lock. This change aims to improve modularity and efficiency by separating concerns at different granularities.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/8] mm/gup: break out gup_lookup_pte() helper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch breaks out the gup_lookup_pte() helper from the larger follow_page_pte() function in mm/gup.c. The new helper resolves a present PTE to the page it maps, returning NULL if the PTE cannot be followed or a negative errno if the caller must report failure. This change simplifies the code and reduces complexity by separating concerns. No functional changes are intended.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 5/8] mm/gup: fill the pages array outside the pud/pmd lock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the huge page handling in the Linux kernel's mm/gup module to fill the pages array and flush caches outside of the pud/pmd lock. The current implementation holds the lock while filling the pages array, which is unnecessary since neither the flush operations nor the page table modifications require exclusive access. By moving the fill operation after unlocking, the patch reduces contention and improves concurrency in the kernel's memory management code.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 6/8] mm/gup: return a huge page's full count from follow_page_mask()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the follow_page_mask() function in the mm/gup module to return the full count of huge pages instead of reporting it via a separate page_mask output. The patch also removes unnecessary code and fixes issues related to error handling and reference counting.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 7/8] mm/gup: walk multiple PTEs per follow_page_pte() call
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the follow_page_pte() function in the Linux kernel's mm/gup.c file by allowing it to walk multiple PTEs per call, rather than one PTE at a time. This reduces the number of page table descents and lock acquisitions, resulting in improved performance for __get_user_pages() calls. The patch was measured to reduce median get times by 2-3x for certain workloads.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 8/8] mm/gup: batch contiguous same-folio PTEs into one refcount grab
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of large folios in the Linux kernel's memory management system by batching contiguous PTEs into a single refcount grab, reducing overhead and improving performance. The patch introduces a new function `gup_pte_batch_len` to determine how many PTEs can be committed as one run, and modifies the `gup_grab_folio_pages` function to take advantage of this optimization. This results in significant performance improvements for large folios, with a 12.8x reduction in execution time for 64 kB mTHP mappings.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/5] memcg: force charges from reclaim before trying the limits
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the memcg (memory cgroup) charging mechanism to force charges from reclaim before trying the limits. This change is necessary because reclaim can charge memory, and if it fails at a limit, it can lead to issues such as increased sleep time for tasks in direct reclaim and kswapd recording overage that it never handles. The patch checks for PF_MEMALLOC before trying the limits, allowing reclaim charges to skip memory.high enforcement and preventing kernel threads from queuing high_work. This change also has effects on how charges are counted and handled by cgroups.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 4/5] memcg: use high_work for remote charges
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a limitation in the memcg (memory cgroup) handling of remote charges, where some charges are directed to a cgroup outside the current task's hierarchy. patches_submitted.patch_summary: The patch addresses a sparse warning on SMP alpha by reading the gid_t inside the kgid_t in kernfs_new_node() and wrapping it back up with KGIDT_INIT(). This change is safe as it does not alter the object code before or after GCC 12 for alpha and GCC 14 for x86-64.

> kernfs_new_node() reads the parent's gid with READ_ONCE(attrs->ia_gid).

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH] x86/lib: Use REP MOVSB for large memcpy() on ERMS CPUs without FSRM
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch optimizes large memory copies on ERMS CPUs without FSRM by using the REP MOVSB instruction, which is more efficient than scalar code. The patch introduces a new threshold of 2048 bytes for using REP MOVSB and keeps scalar code for smaller copies. It also modifies the existing 32-byte check to use REP MOVSB and RET on FSRM CPUs, removing the need for a non-FSRM entry jump. Additionally, it aligns replacement storage before its start label to ensure that the raw FSRM return retains its thunk before relocation. The patch results in significant performance improvements, with a 66.8% reduction in copy time for 4 KiB copies on Cooper Lake CPUs.
